summary: Specifies the media type for carrying PKCS #10 certification requests from RFC 2986. It carries over the specification from RFC 2311, which was moved to Historic. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When you ask a certificate authority for a certificate, the request itself has to travel somewhere. This memo defines the label that says what kind of file it is, so that mail programs and file formats know how to handle it.

subtitle: The media type label for sending a PKCS #10 certificate request, carried over from an old S/MIME RFC.

tldr.problem: The media type for PKCS #10 certificate requests was defined in an S/MIME specification that has since moved to Historic status, and the definition was dropped from the later S/MIME document without being moved anywhere else.
tldr.mechanism: This memo puts the application/pkcs10 definition back, alongside an IANA registration, and links it to the PKCS #10 syntax specification in RFC 2986.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 2986 with the media type definition and the registration, so the registration points at a document that is not Historic.

facts.label: Encoding on output
facts.value: DER preferred; BER or DER accepted on input

today: RFC 5967 is an Informational document from August 2010, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes it and none that updates it. It updates RFC 2986 by adding the application/pkcs10 media type definition and the registration to it, after RFC 2311 moved to Historic status.

sections.title: Why the Media Type Needed a New Home
sections.content:
RFC 2311 first defined the application/pkcs10 media type. When RFC 2633 was published, the application/pkcs10 section was dropped, and for some reason the text was not incorporated into the PKCS #10 document, RFC 2986. RFC 2311 was moved to Historic status by RFC 5751.

To ensure the IANA media type registration points to a non-Historic document, this document updates RFC 2986 with the definition of the application/pkcs10 media type and an IANA registration based on RFC 4288. The text for the section on the body format is adapted from Section 3.7 of RFC 2311.
sections.plainLanguage: The label for certificate requests was first written down in one S/MIME specification. The next S/MIME specification dropped the section, the PKCS #10 specification never picked it up, and the original document was later retired. This memo puts it back in a document that is still current.

sections.title: The Format of the Body
sections.content:
A typical application that lets a user generate cryptographic information has to submit that information to a Certification Authority (CA), which transforms it into a certificate. PKCS #10 (RFC 2986) describes a syntax for certification requests.

The details of certification requests and the process of obtaining a certificate are beyond the scope of this memo. Only the format of the data used in application/pkcs10 is defined. PKCS #10 defines the ASN.1 type CertificationRequest for use in submitting a certification request. For transfer to a CA, this abstract syntax needs to be encoded and identified in a unique manner. When the media type application/pkcs10 is used, the body MUST be a CertificationRequest.

A robust application SHOULD output Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER), but allow Basic Encoding Rules (BER) or DER on input. Data produced by BER or DER is 8-bit, but some transports are limited to 7-bit data. In such cases a suitable 7-bit transfer encoding MUST be applied. In MIME-compatible transports, the base64 encoding (RFC 4648) SHOULD be used with application/pkcs10, although any 7-bit transfer encoding may work.
sections.plainLanguage: The body of the message is one object, the CertificationRequest, and nothing else. The object is written in a standard binary encoding. That encoding uses eight-bit bytes, so on a transport that can only carry seven-bit text, the bytes have to be wrapped in a text-safe encoding first, normally base64.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving the Body
sections.content:
For sending a certificate-signing request, the application/pkcs10 message format MUST be used to convey a PKCS #10 certificate-signing request. For sending certificates and Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) without any signed content, the application/pkcs7-mime message format MUST be used to convey a degenerate PKCS #7 signedData certs-only message (RFC 5751).

To send an application/pkcs10 body, the application generates the cryptographic information for the user. The details of the cryptographic information are beyond the scope of this memo. The process has three steps. First, the cryptographic information is placed within a PKCS #10 CertificationRequest. Second, the CertificationRequest is encoded according to BER or DER, with DER preferred. Third, as a typical step, the encoded CertificationRequest is also base64 encoded so that it is 7-bit data suitable for transfer in ESMTP. That then becomes the body of an application/pkcs10 body part.

A typical application only needs to send a certification request. It is a Certification Authority that has to receive and process the request. The steps for recovering the CertificationRequest from the message are straightforward but are not presented here, and the procedures for processing the certification request are beyond the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Three steps, in order: build the request object, encode it, then wrap it in base64 so it can travel as text. A file of this kind carries a request only. To send an issued certificate or a revocation list, a different format, application/pkcs7-mime, has to be used.

sections.title: The IANA Registration
sections.content:
IANA has updated the registration for the application/pkcs10 media subtype in the Application Media Types registry using the filled-in template from BCP 13 (RFC 4288).

The media subtype for a PKCS #10 certification request is application/pkcs10. The type name is application and the subtype name is pkcs10. Required parameters: none. Optional parameters: none. Encoding considerations: binary, see the section on the body format.

On security, the registration says that clients use a certification request to request that a Certification Authority certify a public key, and that the certification request is digitally signed. On interoperability, it points to the section on the body format. The published specification is this specification. The applications that use this media type are applications that support PKCS #10 certification requests (RFC 2986).

Additional information: magic numbers, none. File extensions: .p10. Macintosh File Type Codes: none given. The person and email address to contact for further information is the author. Restrictions on usage: none. The author is the same person. Intended usage: COMMON. Change controller: the IESG.
sections.plainLanguage: The registration record is short because the format itself is narrow. There are no parameters to set, the file name extension is .p10, and there is no magic number to look for. The intended usage is COMMON, which in the media type registry means the format is expected to be used by many applications.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations of RFC 2986 and RFC 5751 apply. No new security considerations are introduced by this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new. The security rules for certificate requests and for S/MIME messages are the ones already written down, and they carry over unchanged.

data.title: An application/pkcs10 body part
data.code:
Content-Type: application/pkcs10; name=smime.p10
Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64
Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=smime.p10
